summary: This standards-track document specifies several YANG modules that together form the core routing data model, a framework for configuring and managing a routing subsystem. Other YANG modules for specific routing protocols are expected to extend it. This is the NMDA-compatible version of the earlier model.

plainLanguage.summary: Every router needs a notebook of directions. This is a standard notebook layout that other, more specific notebooks can build on.

subtitle: A standard set of YANG modules that describe routes, route tables and routing protocols so any router can be configured the same way.

tldr.problem: Every vendor models routing configuration differently, and more advanced routing features need a common base to build on.
tldr.mechanism: Three YANG modules and one submodule define routes, Routing Information Bases (RIBs) and control-plane protocols, with IPv4 and IPv6 unicast additions. Other modules extend them for specific protocols.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8022 and adapts the model to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).

today: RFC 8349 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018. It obsoletes RFC 8022, and its metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Core Routing Model Is
sections.content:
RFC 8349 specifies three YANG modules and one submodule that together form the core routing data model. The ietf-routing module holds the generic parts. The ietf-ipv4-unicast-routing and ietf-ipv6-unicast-routing modules augment it with data specific to IPv4 and IPv6 unicast. The IPv6 module has a submodule, ietf-ipv6-router-advertisements.

The model is meant as a base. Simple devices that use only static routing can use it directly. Its main purpose is to give building blocks (routes, RIBs and control-plane protocols) to many other modules that IETF working groups are expected to write. The modules conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA), and the document obsoletes RFC 8022.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a shared template for how a router writes down its travel directions. Small routers can use it as is, and fancier routers add pages to it.

sections.title: Design Goals and Structure
sections.content:
The design followed four objectives. The model should suit common address families (IPv4, IPv6) for unicast and multicast routing, as well as MPLS. A simple, static-only router should be configurable without extra modules. The framework must also allow complicated setups with multiple RIBs and multiple control-plane protocols, including controlled redistribution of routing information. Finally, it should be flexible enough for vendors to map onto their own proprietary models.

The top of the tree is a routing container. It holds an optional router-id, a read-only list of interfaces, a list of control-plane-protocols and a list of ribs. The address-family modules attach their own nodes (for example destination-address for the active-route action) by augmenting this tree.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal was one plan that works for a tiny home router and for a huge network machine, and that every maker can fit onto their own gear.

sections.title: System-Controlled and User-Controlled Entries
sections.content:
Some lists, such as rib, must have at least one entry on any working device. The server creates those as system-controlled entries in the operational state. In the RFC's example the /routing/ribs/rib list has two such entries, ipv4-master and ipv6-master.

A client may also create user-controlled entries in the configuration, for example over NETCONF. If the server accepts one, it appears in the operational state too. To add extra settings to a system-controlled entry, the client creates a configuration entry with the same list key.

Deletion differs. Deleting a user-controlled entry from the intended configuration removes the matching operational entry. Deleting a system-controlled entry removes only the extra configuration, and the operational entry stays.
sections.plainLanguage: Some entries are put in the notebook by the router itself and cannot be erased. Others you write in yourself, and you can rub those out.

sections.title: Routes, RIBs and Control-Plane Protocols
sections.content:
A route has a minimal set of attributes. destination-prefix (mandatory) says which destination addresses the route may be used for. route-preference is an integer, also known as administrative distance, used to choose among routes with the same prefix; a lower value is more preferred. next-hop gives the outgoing interface and/or next-hop address, or a special operation to perform on a packet. The special next hops are blackhole, unreachable, prohibit and receive.

A RIB is a list of routes plus administrative data, and each RIB holds routes of only one address family. For every supported address family, exactly one RIB MUST be marked as the default RIB. Implementations that advertise the multiple-ribs feature can have several RIBs per address family, for policy routing and other uses. Each RIB has an active-route action that returns the active route for a given destination address.

A control-plane protocol instance has a type, an identity derived from rt:control-plane-protocol. Two pseudo-protocols are defined: direct and static. They stay on the local device and exchange nothing with neighbors. Every implementation MUST provide exactly one direct instance, which supplies routes to directly connected networks. The static type MAY be configured in zero or more instances.
sections.plainLanguage: A route is one line of directions, like 'for houses on Elm Street, go out the front door'. A RIB is the list of those lines, and a protocol is a way of filling the list.

sections.title: Extending the Model
sections.content:
New control-plane protocols plug in by following a fixed recipe. A new identity MUST be defined whose base is rt:control-plane-protocol or a type derived from it. Extra route attributes MAY be defined, preferably in a YANG grouping, and inserted by augmenting the route node under /rt:routing/rt:ribs/rt:rib/rt:routes/rt:route. Protocol data nodes are added by augmenting control-plane-protocol.

The augmented nodes SHOULD be made conditional with a when statement, valid only when the protocol type matches. The RFC also RECOMMENDS wrapping protocol-specific data in an appropriately named container with presence. Appendix C illustrates all this with an example module for the Routing Information Protocol (RIP), which the RFC describes as an illustration and not a real RIP data model.

The model also depends on switches in other modules. If if:enabled is false for an interface, all routing and forwarding on it MUST be disabled. The ip:ipv4 and ip:ipv6 enabled and forwarding switches work similarly for each IP version.
sections.plainLanguage: If you invent a new way to learn directions, the template tells you exactly where to add your pages so they fit in the notebook.

sections.title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Settings
sections.content:
The ietf-ipv6-router-advertisements submodule augments IPv6 interfaces with the variables that Section 6.2.1 of RFC 4861 requires for Router Advertisements. These include send-advertisements, max-rtr-adv-interval, min-rtr-adv-interval, managed-flag, other-config-flag, link-mtu, reachable-time, retrans-timer, cur-hop-limit, default-lifetime and a prefix-list. Each listed prefix carries valid-lifetime, on-link-flag, preferred-lifetime and autonomous-flag.

The IsRouter flag is implemented by the ip:forwarding leaf in the ietf-ip module. The submodule fixes the valid and preferred lifetimes as constant values across advertisements, because the decrementing behavior that RFC 4861 allows seems problematic and no implementation is known to use it.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router tells nearby computers how to reach it, it announces a list of settings. This part gives each of those settings a standard name you can edit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS over HTTPS for RESTCONF. The NETCONF access control model can limit what users may read or change.

Writable nodes, notably the control-plane-protocol and rib lists, may be sensitive, because unprotected write operations can harm network operations. Reading the rib list may reveal the network topology. The active-route action output could disclose topology or relationships such as client and provider, and the routes a device uses could help mount a later attack on traffic crossing it.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever can change a router's directions can send traffic the wrong way, and whoever can read them learns the map. So only trusted people should get access.

sections.title: Minimum Implementation
sections.content:
Appendix B gives non-normative guidance for a bare minimum, suitable for hosts or very simple routers. It does not support the multiple-ribs feature, so there is a single system-controlled RIB per supported address family (IPv4, IPv6 or both), each also the default RIB, and no user-controlled RIBs. Besides the mandatory direct instance, it should support configuring static instances.

Hosts that never act as routers should drop the ability to send IPv6 Router Advertisements. Resource-constrained platforms may use deviations to restrict the model, for example limiting the number of static instances.
sections.plainLanguage: A small gadget only needs the basic pages of the notebook, so it can skip the fancy ones.

viz.caption: SPECIAL NEXT HOPS DEFINED IN THE ROUTING MODULE

items.label: Unreachable
items.desc: Discard the packet and tell the sender the destination host is unreachable.

items.label: Prohibit
items.desc: Discard the packet and tell the sender that communication is administratively prohibited.

items.label: Receive
items.desc: The packet will be received by the local system.
